title: Commercialism and the Hall's original purpose
summary: Bull objects that crowd-drawing musicians like Sweet Emma are used over better ones, when he thought the Hall was a non-commercial refuge for old musicians.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: You object to the commercialism of the place, is what you're saying, you know?

At the expense of, er, of, of some other musicians, I do, yes. Yeah. I do. I, I object to the fact that some musicians who, er, who are going to draw a crowd are used more than others because they're going to draw a crowd. This, to me, isn't giving equal advantage to New Orleans musicians, which the place, I thought, was supposed to do. Especially when, er, superior musicians are not used there because they don't play an instrument that's acceptable or they, or they haven't got a name that's shrouded in mystery or something. Or a leg shrouded in bells.
Well then, your impression of the place was that it was a non-commercial place designed to, to help New Orleans, musicians in general, not any one particular group or anything.

My impression was that it was, had started out as a non-commercial place to allow these musicians to, er, to keep in practice and keep playing and make money and make a living because most of them are too old to make a living otherwise. And my impression was that it had developed because of its authenticity and because of some mere stroke of luck, it had developed into a successful commercial venture. But I didn't think that it was being run as a commercial venture. I thought that it was a commercial venture in spite of itself. And I'm most disappointed to see that it isn't. And this fact of musicians not being used there because someone down there doesn't like the fellow, or they've had an argument with him, or he doesn't play the right sort of instrument, or he's played across the road at so-and-so's hamburger shop or something like that, that to me is completely bewildering because as far as I'm concerned, if it's a place that is designed to keep alive New Orleans Jazz, the musicianship of the player and the fact that he can play his music and how well he can play it should determine whether or not he works it, whether he's worked over the road, whether he's worked anywhere or whether he plays saxophone or a slide banana.
